questions.q: After the Columbian Exchange, cassava (manioc), a root crop first domesticated in South America, became a staple food in which region?
questions.explain: Portuguese traders carried cassava across the Atlantic in the 1500s, and it became one of the most important food crops of West and Central Africa.

questions.q: To supply workers for the silver mines of Potosi, Spanish officials adapted an Inca system of rotating forced labor. What was it called?
questions.explain: Viceroy Francisco de Toledo organized the mita in the 1570s, forcing Andean communities to send a share of their men to work the mines in rotation.

questions.q: The Ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings at Mesa Verde in present-day Colorado were largely abandoned by about 1300. Which factor is most often cited?
options: A smallpox epidemic spreading from Mexico
Spanish conquest and forced labor drafts
Prolonged drought and strain on resources
Volcanic eruptions in the Rocky Mountains
questions.explain: In the late 1200s Mesa Verde's people migrated south into New Mexico and Arizona during a long drought that strained crops and resources, long before the Spanish arrived.

questions.q: During the 1500s, fishing fleets from France, Portugal, Spain and England crossed the Atlantic each year to catch cod off which region?
options: The mouth of the Chesapeake Bay
questions.explain: After John Cabot reported waters thick with fish in 1497, European fishermen worked the Grand Banks each season, salting and drying cod on nearby shores.

questions.q: In 1599, Juan de Onate's forces destroyed which mesa-top pueblo in New Mexico and then sentenced many surviving men to lose a foot?
questions.explain: After a clash with Onate's soldiers, the Spanish assaulted Acoma, killed hundreds and sentenced survivors to servitude; men over 25 were also sentenced to lose a foot, though how fully that was carried out is debated.

questions.q: The Mexica (Aztecs) fed Tenochtitlan partly with chinampas. What were they?
options: Irrigation canals drawn from desert rivers
Raised plots built up in shallow lake water
Terraced fields carved into steep mountainsides
Stone storehouses that held tribute grain
questions.explain: Chinampas were built from layers of mud and plant matter in the lakes of the Valley of Mexico and produced several harvests a year.

questions.q: In a traditional Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) longhouse, extended families were organized around whom?
options: Related women of a matrilineal clan
The eldest son of the village chief
Priests chosen by the Grand Council
questions.explain: Haudenosaunee society was matrilineal: families in a longhouse were related through women, and clan mothers chose and could remove chiefs.

questions.q: Before Spanish horses spread north, which animal pulled the travois, or pole sled, that Plains peoples used to move camp?
questions.explain: Plains peoples used dogs to haul travois loaded with goods; after horses arrived, larger horse-drawn travois let them carry far more.

questions.q: In the later 1500s, Spain increasingly replaced the encomienda in Mexico with what system, under which Native communities supplied workers in rotation for low wages?
questions.explain: Under the repartimiento, Native towns had to send a share of their men to work for Spanish employers for set periods, in theory for pay.

questions.q: Horses brought by the Spanish in the 1500s were in a sense a return. Why?
options: Native horse species had died out in the Americas long before
The Aztecs had bred small horses only for ceremonies
Horses had survived only in South America's highlands
Viking settlers had brought horses that later vanished entirely
questions.explain: Horses evolved in North America but went extinct there roughly 10,000 years ago; Spanish imports reintroduced them.

questions.q: After the Narvaez expedition was shipwrecked in 1528, which Spaniard spent about eight years crossing the Gulf Coast and Southwest before reaching Mexico?
questions.explain: Cabeza de Vaca and three companions, including the enslaved African Estevanico, lived among Native peoples and finally reached New Spain in 1536.

questions.q: Why did Spanish treasure fleets leaving the Caribbean sail north along the Florida coast before crossing the Atlantic?
options: To trade silver for furs at French trading posts
To avoid ice floes in the southern Atlantic
To ride the Gulf Stream and westerly winds home
To pick up tobacco cargoes in Virginia
questions.explain: The Gulf Stream through the Florida Straits and the westerlies farther north carried ships toward Europe, which is why Spain fortified St. Augustine.

questions.q: From the late 1500s, Spanish galleons regularly carried American silver across the Pacific from Acapulco to which port to buy Asian goods?
questions.explain: The Manila galleons linked Mexico and the Philippines for about 250 years, trading silver for Chinese silk and porcelain.

questions.q: Long before maize arrived, Native peoples of the eastern woodlands domesticated local seed plants such as sunflower and goosefoot. What do archaeologists call this?
questions.explain: Eastern North America was one of the world's independent centers of plant domestication, thousands of years before maize farming spread there.

questions.q: A short-lived 1526 Spanish colony led by Lucas Vazquez de Ayllon on the southeastern coast is notable for what?
options: The first enslaved Africans known in the present-day U.S.
Finding gold in the southern Appalachians
Being the first European colony destroyed by a hurricane
The first Jesuit mission founded in North America
questions.explain: Enslaved Africans at San Miguel de Gualdape rebelled and some fled to live among Native peoples as the colony collapsed within months.

questions.q: Philip II's 1573 Ordinances for founding Spanish towns in the Americas called for what layout?
options: Houses strung along a single river road
Scattered farmsteads with no town center
Streets in a grid around a central plaza
Walled rings around a hilltop fortress
questions.explain: The ordinances, part of the Laws of the Indies, set the plaza-and-grid plan seen in towns from St. Augustine to Santa Fe.

questions.q: In the 1500s, Basque whalers built a large seasonal whaling station at Red Bay, on the coast of what is now which place?
questions.explain: Red Bay, Labrador, is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site; Basque crews rendered whale oil there for European markets.

questions.q: Which food did the Ojibwe and other peoples of the western Great Lakes harvest from shallow lakes by canoe?
questions.explain: Harvesters knocked the grain of wild rice, or manoomin, into their canoes; it remains culturally central to the Ojibwe.

questions.q: Texas longhorn cattle descend largely from animals first brought to the Americas by which colonizers?
questions.explain: Spanish cattle introduced in the Caribbean and Mexico in the 1500s spread north and ran semi-wild in Texas, later fueling the cattle drives.

questions.q: The great houses of Chaco Canyon in New Mexico, built by Ancestral Puebloans between about 850 and 1150, were linked to outlying communities by what?
questions.explain: The Chacoan roads run for miles in straight lines across the desert and are part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.q: Which Mesoamerican product, whose beans the Aztecs also used as money, became a fashionable drink in Europe after the conquest?
questions.explain: Europeans adopted chocolate drinks and added sugar; coffee and tea came from Africa and Asia, and mate from South America.

questions.q: Which bird, domesticated by Native peoples of Mexico, was carried to Europe in the Columbian Exchange?
questions.explain: Turkeys were domesticated in Mesoamerica and reached Europe in the early 1500s; chickens came to the Americas from the Old World.

questions.q: Cuitlahuac, who became Aztec ruler after Moctezuma II and led the resistance that drove the Spanish from Tenochtitlan in 1520, died after only about 80 days as ruler. What killed him?
questions.explain: Smallpox, probably carried by a member of Narvaez's force, swept Tenochtitlan in late 1520, killing many, including Cuitlahuac, and weakening the city before the 1521 siege.

questions.q: Tree-ring studies published in 1998 found that Jamestown's first years, 1606 to 1612, coincided with what?
options: The worst drought in about 770 years
A volcanic winter that froze the James River
An unusually warm and wet growing season
A hurricane that flooded the fort
questions.explain: The severe drought helps explain the colony's food shortages, bad water and tensions with the Powhatan, who also faced crop failures.

questions.q: North Carolina's longleaf pine forests made the colony a leading producer of what for British shipbuilding?
questions.explain: These naval stores, made from pine resin, sealed wooden ships and rigging; Parliament paid bounties to encourage them.

questions.q: Massachusetts's 1691 charter reserved the colony's largest white pines for the Crown. What were the trees meant for?
questions.explain: Surveyors marked such trees with the king's broad arrow; colonists' resentment of the policy flared in incidents like the 1772 Pine Tree Riot.

questions.q: The Pennsylvania Dutch who settled in colonial Pennsylvania mostly came from where?
options: The Dutch Republic and Spanish Flanders
questions.explain: Dutch here comes from Deutsch, meaning German; these immigrants included Lutherans, Reformed, Mennonites and Amish.

questions.q: Many German immigrants of the 1700s were redemptioners. What did that mean?
options: They paid in advance for land near Philadelphia
They were ransomed captives freed from pirates
They sold their labor on arrival to repay passage
They served as soldiers in exchange for land
questions.explain: Redemptioners sailed without paying and had a short time after landing to raise the fare; if they could not, their labor was sold for a term of years.

questions.q: In 1734, Protestant refugees from Salzburg, expelled by their Catholic archbishop, founded the settlement of Ebenezer in which colony?
questions.explain: The Salzburgers were among Georgia's earliest settlers and became known for opposing the introduction of slavery there.

questions.q: The 23 Jewish refugees who reached New Amsterdam in 1654, founding the first Jewish community in North America, had fled from where?
questions.explain: When Portugal retook Recife from the Dutch, Sephardic Jews there left; the group that reached New Amsterdam founded Congregation Shearith Israel.

questions.q: In his 1751 essay Observations Concerning the Increase of Mankind, Benjamin Franklin explained the colonies' fast population growth mainly by what?
options: Cheap land that let people marry young
questions.explain: Franklin argued that plentiful land let colonists start families early, so the population doubled about every 20 years.

questions.q: In 1600s Virginia and New England, a frequent source of conflict between colonists and Native peoples was what?
options: Disputes over who could fish in the Atlantic
Competition to sell maize to Spanish Florida
Colonists' free-roaming hogs and cattle eating Native crops
Native refusal to trade any furs with the English
questions.explain: English livestock roamed unfenced and trampled or ate Native cornfields, and colonists treated the animals as property even on Native land.

questions.q: Why did towns such as Richmond, Georgetown and Philadelphia grow up along the fall line?
options: It marked the limit of the Proclamation Line
It stopped seagoing ships and offered water power
It held the colonies' richest gold deposits
It was the only place free of malaria
questions.explain: The fall line, where rivers drop from the Piedmont to the coastal plain, made a natural transfer point for goods and a site for mills.

questions.q: In the 1737 Walking Purchase, Pennsylvania officials used trained runners to claim a vast tract from which people?
questions.explain: Relying on a disputed old deed for land as far as a man could walk in a day and a half, the fastest runner, Edward Marshall, covered about 65 miles.

questions.q: European demand for which fashion item drove the North American beaver trade in the 1600s?
questions.explain: Beaver underfur made the best felt for hats, and the fashion fueled the French, Dutch and English fur trades.

questions.q: Georgia's founders banned slavery in the colony in 1735. In which year did slavery become legal there?
questions.explain: Settlers pressed for enslaved labor to compete with South Carolina; after the ban was lifted effective January 1, 1751, Georgia rapidly became a plantation colony.

questions.q: By about 1720, what was distinctive about South Carolina's population?
options: Native peoples made up most of Charleston
It had no enslaved people at all
questions.explain: Rice cultivation drove massive imports of enslaved Africans, making South Carolina the only mainland colony with a Black majority for much of the century.

questions.q: Parliament's Currency Act of 1751 restricted which colonies from issuing paper money as legal tender?
questions.explain: Merchants in Britain complained that New England's paper money had depreciated; a broader Currency Act followed in 1764.

questions.q: Beginning in 1718, Britain shipped tens of thousands of whom to the colonies, mostly to Maryland and Virginia?
questions.explain: About 50,000 convicts were transported to the American colonies under an act of Parliament before the Revolution ended the practice.

questions.q: Moravian settlers who founded Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, in 1741 later built which planned town in North Carolina?
questions.explain: Salem, founded in 1766 on the Moravians' Wachovia tract, merged with neighboring Winston in 1913.

questions.q: Under New France's seigneurial system, farms along the St. Lawrence River were laid out how?
options: As walled plantations around a central house
As long, narrow strips running back from the river
As common fields shared by a whole village
questions.explain: Narrow lots gave each family river frontage for transport and fishing; the pattern is still visible in Quebec and Louisiana.

questions.q: William Penn's 1682 plan for Philadelphia was notable for what?
options: Winding lanes around a central stone fort
A street grid with five public squares
A town wall against Native attack
questions.explain: Penn and surveyor Thomas Holme laid out a grid between the Delaware and Schuylkill rivers with a central square and four others.

questions.q: What was a main goal of the Haudenosaunee mourning wars of the 1600s?
options: Driving the Dutch out of the Hudson Valley
Forcing the Huron to accept Catholicism
Seizing European ports to control the fur trade
Taking captives to replace people lost to disease and war
questions.explain: Epidemics devastated the Haudenosaunee, and raids brought captives who were adopted to fill the places of the dead.

questions.q: After smallpox killed many Native people near Massachusetts Bay in 1633-1634, how did Governor John Winthrop interpret the epidemic?
options: As God clearing the colonists' title to the land
As proof that Native medicine was superior
As a sign that the colony should move inland
As punishment for colonists' trade with the Dutch
questions.explain: Winthrop wrote that the Lord had cleared their title to what they possessed, a view that justified taking Native land.

questions.q: Many Algonquian peoples of southern New England moved among several sites during the year. What was the main reason?
options: To trade at a different English town each season
To use seasonal food sources such as fish runs, crops and game
To escape the summer heat of the coastal plain
To avoid paying tribute to the Haudenosaunee
questions.explain: Historian William Cronon showed how seasonal movement between coast, fields and hunting grounds clashed with English ideas of fixed property.

questions.q: In the later 1700s, South Carolina rice planters increasingly moved production to tidal swamps along rivers. What did this setting allow?
options: Growing rice without any enslaved labor at all
Using the tides to flood and drain fields through gates
Harvesting a second crop of wheat each winter
Shipping rice to China directly from the plantations
questions.explain: Enslaved workers built banks, ditches and floodgates so freshwater pushed upriver by the tides could irrigate the fields, a huge and dangerous labor effort.

questions.q: The Dutch founded Fort Orange in 1624 on the upper Hudson River, at the site of present-day Albany, mainly to do what?
options: Mine iron ore for Dutch shipyards
Guard against Spanish raids from Florida
Trade with Native peoples for furs
questions.explain: Fort Orange drew Mohawk and Mahican traders with beaver pelts; the town that grew around it became Beverwijck and later Albany.

questions.q: In early 1777, George Washington ordered what for Continental Army recruits who had never had smallpox?
questions.explain: Washington's decision to inoculate the army is credited with protecting it during a continent-wide epidemic; Jenner's cowpox vaccine came only in 1796.

questions.q: A 1793 yellow fever epidemic killed about a tenth of the population of which city, then the nation's capital?
questions.explain: About 5,000 died; members of the Free African Society, led by Richard Allen and Absalom Jones, nursed the sick and buried the dead.

questions.q: In 1775, Daniel Boone led axmen to blaze which route through the Cumberland Gap into Kentucky?
questions.explain: Some 200,000 or more settlers used the Wilderness Road to cross the Appalachians by the early 1800s.

questions.q: Western Pennsylvania farmers in the 1790s distilled much of their grain into whiskey mainly because of what?
options: Federal law required grain to be distilled
Whiskey was far cheaper to ship over the mountains
Whiskey was the only legal currency
Eastern cities had banned grain imports
questions.explain: Bulky grain was costly to haul east, so whiskey served as a portable product and even money, which is why the 1791 excise tax hit so hard.

questions.q: In the 1780s, Delaware inventor Oliver Evans designed what?
options: A steam-powered riverboat for the Ohio
questions.explain: Evans's mill moved grain through every step with elevators and conveyors, an early example of continuous automated production.

questions.q: The 1768 Treaty of Fort Stanwix, signed by the Haudenosaunee, opened land south of the Ohio River in Kentucky. Which nation, which hunted there, rejected it?
questions.explain: The Haudenosaunee ceded land they did not occupy, and Shawnee anger over settlement there helped lead to Lord Dunmore's War in 1774.

questions.q: Many Acadians expelled by the British from Nova Scotia beginning in 1755 eventually resettled where, becoming known as Cajuns?
questions.explain: During the Great Expulsion, thousands were deported; many later moved to Spanish Louisiana, where Acadian became Cajun.

questions.q: Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon surveyed their famous line in the 1760s to settle a boundary dispute between which colonies?
questions.explain: Their survey, finished in 1767, ended an old dispute between the Penn and Calvert families; the line later symbolized the divide between free and slave states.

questions.q: In 1769 Spain began building missions in Alta California, starting at San Diego. Which Franciscan led the effort?
questions.explain: Serra founded nine of California's 21 missions; Native people were drawn into forced labor there, and disease cut their numbers sharply.

questions.q: Under the Land Ordinance of 1785, federal land was first sold in minimum lots of what size, which favored speculators?
questions.explain: At a minimum of $1 an acre, a 640-acre purchase was beyond most farmers; later land laws steadily cut the minimum size.

questions.q: Marietta, the first permanent American settlement in the Northwest Territory, was founded in 1788 by which group?
questions.explain: Revolutionary War veterans in the Ohio Company bought a large tract from Congress and settled at the mouth of the Muskingum River.

questions.q: The 1790 Treaty of New York, signed in the temporary capital, was negotiated with Alexander McGillivray, a leader of which nation?
questions.explain: The Creek ceded some Georgia lands, and the U.S. guaranteed the rest of their territory, a promise Georgia settlers soon ignored.

questions.q: In 1784, the Empress of China sailed from New York to open American trade with which port?
questions.explain: Free of British trade limits after independence, American merchants traded ginseng and silver for tea, silk and porcelain at Canton (Guangzhou).

questions.q: In 1792, American trader Robert Gray, seeking sea otter furs for the China trade, became the first non-Native to sail into which river?
questions.explain: Gray named the river for his ship, the Columbia Rediviva, and his voyage later supported U.S. claims to the Oregon Country.

questions.q: The first U.S. census, taken in 1790, counted a total population of about how many people?
questions.explain: The census, required by the Constitution to apportion House seats, was conducted by federal marshals.

questions.q: Critics mocked the Erie Canal as a ditch named after which New York governor who championed it?
questions.explain: Clinton's Ditch proved a huge success after it opened in 1825, with Clinton again serving as governor.

questions.q: The Preemption Act of 1841 allowed squatters on federal land to do what?
options: Claim land for free after living on it five years
Buy up to 160 acres at the minimum price before auction
Sell their claims to railroads at market value
Vote in territorial elections without owning land
questions.explain: The law recognized settlers who had moved onto surveyed public land, letting them buy at $1.25 an acre before it went to public sale.

questions.q: Francis Cabot Lowell helped launch the New England textile industry after doing what on a visit to Britain?
options: Memorizing the design of British power looms
Hiring away a famous British engineer
Buying a mill and shipping it to Boston
questions.explain: Britain banned exporting textile machinery, so Lowell studied the looms closely and rebuilt them in Waltham with mechanic Paul Moody.

questions.q: German refugees who came to the U.S. after the failed revolutions of 1848, such as Carl Schurz, became known as what?
questions.explain: Many Forty-Eighters were educated liberals who opposed slavery, joined the Republican Party and served in the Union army.

questions.q: The name Black Belt, for the cotton region across central Alabama and Mississippi, originally referred to what?
questions.explain: The rich prairie soils drew planters and enslaved workers in the cotton boom; the term later also described the region's large Black population.

questions.q: Most Oregon Trail emigrants of the 1840s aimed for farmland in which valley?
questions.explain: Reports of rich soil and mild climate in the Willamette Valley helped spark Oregon fever.

questions.q: Mexico granted Stephen F. Austin and other empresarios land in Texas in the 1820s on condition that they did what?
options: Paid annual rent to the Comanche nation
Built forts to guard the Louisiana border
Brought in settlers who would become Mexican citizens
Freed all enslaved people they brought with them
questions.explain: Settlers were expected to become Mexican citizens and Catholics, but the fast-growing American population soon clashed with Mexican authorities.

questions.q: From 1825 to 1840, trappers in the Rocky Mountains met fur company traders each summer at a gathering called what?
questions.explain: The rendezvous replaced fixed trading posts; trappers swapped pelts for supplies until the beaver trade collapsed around 1840.

questions.q: After his 1820 expedition, Major Stephen Long described the Great Plains in terms that popularized which label?
questions.explain: Long called the region almost wholly unfit for cultivation, and his map marked it as desert; the idea helped justify placing removed Native nations there.

questions.q: Henry Shreve's steamboat designs of the 1810s suited western rivers because they had what?
options: Iron hulls that could break ice
Shallow hulls with engines on the main deck
Twin sails to supplement their steam engines
questions.explain: Shreve's shallow-draft boats could navigate the Mississippi and Ohio; he also cleared the Red River's Great Raft, and Shreveport bears his name.

questions.q: The 1838 Trail of Death forced which nation from northern Indiana to present-day Kansas?
questions.explain: About 850 Potawatomi were marched under militia guard; about 40, many of them children, died on the way.

questions.q: Cholera epidemics that struck American cities in 1832 and 1849 spread mainly through what?
questions.explain: Crowded cities lacked sewers and clean water; the link to contaminated water was not shown until John Snow's work in London in 1854.

questions.q: In 1844, Charles Goodyear patented a process that made rubber stay firm in heat and flexible in cold. What is it called?
questions.explain: Heating rubber with sulfur transformed a sticky material into a useful one for boots, belts and later tires.

questions.q: Sarah Bagley organized the Lowell Female Labor Reform Association in 1845 chiefly to campaign for what?
questions.explain: Mill women petitioned the Massachusetts legislature for a ten-hour day; Bagley testified before a legislative committee in 1845.

questions.q: From the 1830s until the Civil War, what was the leading U.S. export by value?
questions.explain: By 1860 cotton made up more than half of all U.S. exports, feeding the textile mills of Britain and New England.

questions.q: After arriving in 1847, Mormon settlers made the dry Salt Lake Valley farmable mainly by doing what?
options: Drilling deep wells powered by windmills and steam
Digging shared irrigation ditches from mountain creeks
Draining marshes along the Great Salt Lake
Waiting for rainfall to rise with plowing
questions.explain: Church-organized irrigation diverted creeks from the Wasatch Mountains, a model of cooperative water use in the arid West.

questions.q: Many German immigrants of the 1840s and 1850s settled in a German triangle anchored by which cities?
questions.explain: German newcomers in these Midwestern cities built breweries, newspapers, churches and schools in their own language.

questions.q: The Santa Fe Trail opened in 1821 after which event made trade with New Mexico legal?
questions.explain: Spain had barred American traders, but independent Mexico welcomed them, and wagons soon carried goods between Missouri and Santa Fe.

questions.q: Elias Howe patented which device in 1846, which Isaac Singer later improved and sold widely?
questions.explain: Howe won a patent fight with Singer, and the machine reshaped garment work in homes and factories.

questions.q: The Erie Canal connected the Hudson River at Albany with Lake Erie at which city?
questions.explain: The 363-mile canal turned Buffalo into a major port where Great Lakes grain moved onto canal boats bound for New York City.

questions.q: In 1844, deadly nativist riots broke out in which city over disputes about which Bible Catholic children used in public schools?
questions.explain: Mobs burned two Catholic churches in May, St. Michael's in Kensington and St. Augustine's, and deadly fighting followed in Southwark in July; the riots fed the rise of the Know-Nothings.

questions.q: Historians estimate that roughly how many enslaved people were forcibly moved from the Upper South to the Deep South between 1790 and 1860?
questions.explain: This forced migration, sometimes called the Second Middle Passage, broke up families as cotton expanded west.

questions.q: Besides acquiring Florida, the Adams-Onis Treaty of 1819 did what?
options: Settled the border with British Canada
Drew a U.S.-Spanish boundary to the Pacific
questions.explain: Spain gave up its claims to Oregon, and the U.S. gave up claims to Texas, along a stepped line ending at the 42nd parallel.

questions.q: The Ohio and Erie Canal, completed in 1832, linked Lake Erie at Cleveland with which river?
questions.explain: Running to Portsmouth, the canal connected Ohio farms to both the Great Lakes and the Mississippi system, and Cleveland boomed.

questions.q: President John Quincy Adams broke ground in 1828 for the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal, which ran along which river?
questions.explain: The canal reached Cumberland, Maryland, in 1850 but never got to the Ohio; the faster railroad overtook it.

questions.q: California's 1852 Foreign Miners' Tax, a monthly license fee, fell most heavily on which group?
questions.explain: An 1850 version had driven out many Mexican and Chilean miners; the 1852 tax mainly targeted the Chinese and brought the state large revenues.

questions.q: The Comstock Lode, discovered in 1859, was a huge deposit of silver in what is now which state?
questions.explain: The strike created Virginia City and helped Nevada gain statehood in 1864.

questions.q: The 1858-1859 gold rush known by the slogan Pikes Peak or Bust led to the founding of which city?
questions.explain: Tens of thousands of fortune seekers rushed to the Rockies, and mining camps at the mouth of Cherry Creek grew into Denver.

questions.q: After the U.S.-Dakota War of 1862 in Minnesota, 38 Dakota men were hanged at Mankato. What distinction does this event hold?
options: The largest mass execution in U.S. history
The first execution ordered by the Supreme Court
The only execution approved by Congress
The last public hanging in the United States
questions.explain: A military commission condemned 303 men; Lincoln reviewed the trials and approved 39 death sentences, and 38 were hanged on December 26, 1862.

questions.q: Which federal department did Lincoln sign into existence in 1862, later calling it the people's department?
questions.explain: Most Americans then farmed; the new agency spread research and seeds, and gained cabinet rank in 1889.

questions.q: In 1864, Lincoln signed a law granting Yosemite Valley and the Mariposa Grove of giant sequoias to whom, for public use?
questions.explain: The Yosemite Grant was the first time the federal government set aside scenic land for public enjoyment, a precedent for later national parks.

questions.q: George Perkins Marsh's 1864 book Man and Nature is often seen as a founding text of American conservation because it argued what?
options: Wild lands belonged to Native nations alone
Human activity could badly damage the environment
Nature would always recover without help
Forests should be cleared to improve the climate
questions.explain: Marsh, a Vermont diplomat, showed how deforestation and overuse had ruined lands around the Mediterranean and warned Americans.

questions.q: Starting in 1867, Texas ranchers drove cattle north along the Chisholm Trail to railheads at which Kansas town?
questions.explain: Joseph McCoy built stockyards at Abilene on the Kansas Pacific line, and cattle were shipped east to Chicago.

questions.q: The Southern Homestead Act of 1866 opened public land in five Southern states mainly to whom, at first?
questions.explain: For its first months the law barred former Confederates; much of the land was poor, and few freedpeople ended up with farms.

questions.q: During and after the Gold Rush, California's Native population fell from roughly 150,000 in 1848 to about how many by 1870?
questions.explain: Disease, starvation, forced labor and organized killings, some paid for by the state, caused one of the worst population collapses in U.S. history.

questions.q: The Burlingame Treaty of 1868 with China did what?
options: Gave the U.S. a permanent naval base near Shanghai
Opened Japan's ports to American ships
Affirmed Chinese people's right to migrate to the U.S.
Banned Chinese laborers from entering the U.S.
questions.explain: Railroads wanted Chinese labor, and the treaty affirmed free migration; Congress reversed course with the Chinese Exclusion Act in 1882.

questions.q: In the Long Walk of 1864, Navajo people were forced to march to Bosque Redondo, a reservation beside which fort?
questions.explain: Crops failed and many died at Bosque Redondo; the Treaty of 1868 let the Navajo return to part of their homeland.

questions.q: The 1851 Treaty of Fort Laramie sought mainly to do what?
options: End the Mexican-American War on the northern frontier
Protect emigrant trails by setting tribal boundaries
Create a single reservation for all Plains peoples
Sell the Black Hills to the United States
questions.explain: The U.S. promised annuities in return for letting emigrants and forts along the trails pass safely, but the peace soon broke down.

questions.q: After emancipation, why did many freedpeople place Information Wanted advertisements in newspapers?
options: To find relatives separated by slavery
To recruit workers for Northern factories
To sell land given by the Freedmen's Bureau
questions.explain: Thousands of such ads, many in Black newspapers, sought spouses, children and parents sold away, sometimes decades earlier.

questions.q: Under the California Land Act of 1851, Californio landowners had to do what to keep their ranchos?
options: Become Protestant and swear loyalty oaths
Prove their old land titles before a federal board
Sell part of their land to the railroad
Pay a fee equal to half the land's value
questions.explain: Lengthy, costly proceedings forced many Californios to sell or lose land, even when their claims were upheld.

questions.q: Edwin Drake drilled the first commercially successful U.S. oil well in 1859 near which Pennsylvania town?
questions.explain: Drake's well set off an oil rush in western Pennsylvania; kerosene for lamps was the main product at first.

questions.q: Under the Timber Culture Act of 1873, a settler on the Plains could gain 160 acres by doing what?
options: Planting trees on part of the land
Grazing cattle there for ten years
Building a church or school on it
Fencing the land with barbed wire
questions.explain: Congress hoped trees would change the climate and supply timber; settlers had to plant 40 acres of trees, later reduced to 10.

questions.q: The Desert Land Act of 1877 offered settlers 640 acres at $1.25 an acre if they did what within three years?
questions.explain: The law was widely abused by cattle companies and speculators who made only token efforts at irrigation.

questions.q: John Wesley Powell's 1878 Report on the Lands of the Arid Region argued what about the West?
options: Scarce water should shape how land was divided and settled
The West would become rainy once it was farmed
Western land should be reserved for Native nations
The region's future lay mainly in silver mining
questions.explain: Powell urged larger grazing units and irrigation districts based on available water; Congress largely ignored him.

questions.q: In 1869, one-armed Civil War veteran John Wesley Powell led the first known expedition down which river through the Grand Canyon?
questions.explain: Powell's party began on the Green River in Wyoming and ran the Colorado through the Grand Canyon in wooden boats.

questions.q: The popular theory of the 1870s and 1880s that rain follows the plow claimed what?
options: Farming the Plains would bring more rain
Rainfall would decrease as towns grew
Plowed fields would dry out the soil
questions.explain: An unusually wet period seemed to support the idea, which drew settlers west until severe droughts in the late 1880s and 1890s.

questions.q: With few trees on the Great Plains, many homesteaders built their first homes from what?
options: Adobe bricks made of desert clay
questions.explain: Sod houses, sometimes called soddies, were cheap and well insulated but leaked and were hard to keep clean.

questions.q: Mennonite immigrants from Russia are credited with bringing Turkey Red, a hardy variety of which crop, to Kansas in the 1870s?
questions.explain: Turkey Red handled the cold winters and dry summers of the Plains and helped make Kansas a leading wheat state.

questions.q: Which technology let Plains homesteaders pump groundwater where streams were scarce?
questions.explain: Cheap, self-regulating windmills dotted the Plains by the 1880s, watering homes and livestock.

questions.q: The brutal winter of 1886-1887 on the northern Plains had what major effect?
options: It drove the last bison herds into Canada
It killed huge numbers of cattle and ended the open-range boom
It ended the Lakota resistance on the Plains
It froze the Missouri River and halted the railroads for a year
questions.explain: After overgrazing and a dry summer, blizzards killed many cattle; ranchers turned to fenced land and winter hay.

questions.q: The 1889 Johnstown Flood in Pennsylvania, which killed more than 2,200 people, was caused by what?
options: Spring ice jams on the nearby Ohio River
A breach in the Pennsylvania Canal
The failure of a poorly maintained dam upstream
A hurricane that came up the Chesapeake
questions.explain: The South Fork Dam held a lake for a private club of wealthy Pittsburgh businessmen; when it failed, a wall of water hit the town.

questions.q: Which city burned in an 1871 fire that left about 100,000 people homeless?
questions.explain: The Great Chicago Fire destroyed much of the city's center, and rebuilding in brick and steel made Chicago a center of modern architecture.

questions.q: On the same night as the Great Chicago Fire in October 1871, which Wisconsin blaze became the deadliest wildfire in U.S. history?
questions.explain: Logging slash and drought fed the Peshtigo Fire, which killed an estimated 1,200 to 2,400 people.

questions.q: Woodruff v. North Bloomfield (1884), a federal court case, effectively halted what practice in California?
options: Dumping hydraulic mining debris into rivers
Hunting sea otters for their fur
questions.explain: Hydraulic mining washed hillsides into streams, burying farms and clogging rivers; Judge Lorenzo Sawyer banned dumping the debris.

questions.q: Arbor Day was first celebrated in 1872 in which treeless Plains state, where about a million trees were planted that day?
questions.explain: Newspaper editor J. Sterling Morton promoted the holiday, and Nebraska later took the nickname the Tree Planters' State.

questions.q: Many Italian immigrant laborers in the late 1800s found work through padrones. Who were they?
options: Officials who inspected arrivals at Ellis Island
Parish priests who ran charity hospitals
Union leaders who organized dock strikes
Labor brokers who arranged jobs for a cut of wages
questions.explain: Padrones often spoke English and found railroad and construction work for newcomers, but many exploited them.

questions.q: A major push factor for Jewish emigration from the Russian Empire after 1881 was what?
options: A famine caused by potato blight
questions.explain: After the assassination of Alexander II, waves of mob violence and restrictive laws drove well over a million Jews from the Russian Empire to the U.S. by the 1920s.

questions.q: The dumbbell tenement design used in New York after an 1879 law was meant to give every room what?
options: A window, through narrow air shafts
Gas lighting and central steam heat
questions.explain: The narrow airshafts rarely gave real light or air and spread fire and noise; a stronger 1901 law banned new dumbbells.

questions.q: Frank Sprague's 1888 electric streetcar system in Richmond, Virginia, helped American cities grow in what way?
options: Into streetcar suburbs along trolley lines
questions.explain: Within a few years most U.S. cities had electric trolleys, letting middle-class families live farther from downtown.

questions.q: When it opened in 1883, the Brooklyn Bridge was the world's longest bridge of what type?
questions.explain: Designed by John A. Roebling and finished by his son Washington and Emily Warren Roebling, it used steel wire cables.

questions.q: Gustavus Swift's refrigerated railroad cars of the late 1870s let meatpackers in which city ship fresh beef nationwide?
questions.explain: Shipping dressed beef instead of live cattle cut costs and helped make Chicago's Union Stock Yards the center of the meat industry.

questions.q: In the 1885 Rock Springs massacre in Wyoming Territory, white miners killed at least 28 of which group of fellow workers?
questions.explain: Resentful that the Union Pacific coal company employed Chinese workers at lower pay, a mob attacked them and burned their homes.

questions.q: The Molly Maguires, a secret group accused of violence in the 1870s, were Irish coal miners in which region?
questions.explain: Based largely on a Pinkerton agent's testimony, twenty men were hanged; coming after the failed 1875 Long Strike, the trials crushed labor organizing in the region.

questions.q: Norwegian and Swedish immigrants of the late 1800s settled most heavily in which region?
questions.explain: Cheap land and a familiar climate drew Scandinavians to the upper Midwest, where many farmed.

questions.q: To sell their land grants, western railroads in the 1870s and 1880s sent agents to recruit settlers mainly from where?
questions.explain: Lines like the Northern Pacific and Santa Fe advertised in Germany and Scandinavia, offering cheap fares and land on credit.

questions.q: The Hatch Act of 1887 funded what at land-grant colleges?
questions.explain: The stations researched crops, soils and livestock; this Hatch Act is different from the 1939 law limiting federal workers' political activity.

questions.q: The Second Morrill Act of 1890 led to the founding of many colleges for whom?
options: Black students in the segregated South
Native American students in the West
questions.explain: States that kept Black students out of existing land-grant colleges had to provide separate ones, creating many historically Black land-grant schools.

questions.q: The Mesabi Range, which opened in the 1890s and soon became the nation's leading source of iron ore, is in which state?
questions.explain: Its soft ore could be scooped up by steam shovels and shipped across the Great Lakes to steel mills.

questions.q: The Lacey Act of 1900, the first federal law protecting wildlife, banned what?
options: The import of all foreign plants and seeds
Interstate shipment of illegally killed animals
All hunting of wild birds for hat feathers
questions.explain: Congressman John Lacey's law targeted market hunters who killed game in violation of state laws and shipped it across state lines.

questions.q: In 1903, Theodore Roosevelt made Florida's Pelican Island the first of what?
questions.explain: Plume hunters were killing birds for hat feathers; Roosevelt went on to create more than 50 bird reservations.

questions.q: The Weeks Act of 1911 allowed the federal government to do what?
options: Lease western grazing land to ranchers
Sell timber from national parks to mills
Buy eastern private land for national forests
questions.explain: Most eastern forest land was privately owned and heavily logged; the act helped create national forests in the Appalachians and White Mountains.

questions.q: In Missouri v. Holland (1920), the Supreme Court upheld a federal law protecting what, based on the treaty power?
questions.explain: The Migratory Bird Treaty Act carried out a 1916 treaty with Britain for Canada; Justice Holmes ruled a treaty could support laws Congress might not pass otherwise.

questions.q: The Big Burn of August 1910, which scorched about 3 million acres in Idaho and Montana, led the Forest Service to adopt what?
options: A policy of putting out all wildfires quickly
A ban on all logging in the Rockies
Controlled burning in every national forest
Transfer of fire control to the states
questions.explain: The disaster built support for the young Forest Service and a total fire suppression policy, later criticized for building up fuel.

questions.q: Martha, who died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1914, was the last known member of which species, once perhaps the most numerous bird in North America?
questions.explain: Commercial hunting and forest clearing wiped out flocks once numbering in the billions; Martha's body went to the Smithsonian.

questions.q: The Great Mississippi Flood of 1927 led Congress to pass the Flood Control Act of 1928, which did what?
options: Banned farming on the Mississippi floodplain
Made lower Mississippi flood control a federal job
questions.explain: The Army Corps of Engineers took charge of a system of levees, spillways and floodways on the lower river.

questions.q: Which Commerce Secretary directed relief after the 1927 Mississippi flood, raising his profile before the 1928 presidential race?
questions.explain: Hoover organized Red Cross relief camps; Black refugees suffered discrimination and forced labor in some camps.

questions.q: The Taylor Grazing Act of 1934 did what on western public lands?
options: Gave them to the states to sell
Set up grazing districts run by permit
questions.explain: Overgrazing had damaged the range; the law effectively ended homesteading on much of the remaining public domain.

questions.q: Franklin Roosevelt's Shelterbelt Project in the 1930s planted millions of trees across the Plains to do what?
options: Supply timber for New Deal housing
Mark the borders of Native reservations
Break the wind and slow soil erosion
questions.explain: Workers planted more than 200 million trees in belts from North Dakota to Texas in response to the Dust Bowl.

questions.q: After the 1900 hurricane that killed some 6,000 to 12,000 people in Galveston, Texas, how did the city protect itself?
options: Built a seawall and raised the city's ground level
Moved the whole city ten miles inland to the mainland
Dredged a canal to drain the island
questions.explain: The storm remains the deadliest natural disaster in U.S. history; Galveston also pioneered the commission form of city government.

questions.q: Most of the destruction from the 1906 San Francisco earthquake was caused by what?
options: Fires that burned for days afterward
A tsunami that swept over the waterfront
questions.explain: Broken water mains left firefighters helpless, and the fires destroyed about 28,000 buildings.

questions.q: The Los Angeles Aqueduct, completed in 1913 under engineer William Mulholland, drew water from which valley, angering its farmers?
questions.explain: Los Angeles quietly bought up water rights; Owens Valley ranchers later dynamited parts of the aqueduct in protest.

questions.q: Grand Coulee and Bonneville dams, built during the New Deal, harnessed which river for power and irrigation?
questions.explain: Their electricity later powered wartime aluminum plants and aircraft factories; Woody Guthrie wrote songs promoting the project.

questions.q: Dust Bowl migrants who headed to California in the 1930s were often given what nickname?
questions.explain: The label, often used as an insult, applied to migrants from Oklahoma and neighboring states.

questions.q: In the Mexican Repatriation of the early 1930s, what happened to many people of Mexican descent?
options: Hundreds of thousands, many U.S. citizens, were pushed out
Most gained citizenship through a New Deal program
They were recruited to build western dams
They were drafted into the Civilian Conservation Corps
questions.explain: Local, state and federal officials used raids and pressure; estimates range from about 400,000 to more than a million people.

questions.q: During the first Great Migration, Black migrants from Mississippi most often headed to which city, along the Illinois Central Railroad?
questions.explain: Migrants tended to follow rail lines north; Chicago's Black population grew more than fivefold between 1910 and 1930.

questions.q: Besides promising Philippine independence, the Tydings-McDuffie Act of 1934 limited Filipino immigration to how many people a year?
questions.explain: Filipinos had moved freely as U.S. nationals; the act reclassified them as aliens and set one of the smallest quotas.

questions.q: Congress created Yosemite National Park in 1890 around the state-run Yosemite Valley. In what year did California give the valley back to the federal government?
questions.explain: John Muir and the Sierra Club campaigned for unified federal control, and Theodore Roosevelt signed the bill accepting the valley in 1906.

questions.q: The Love Canal neighborhood, evacuated in 1978-1980 after buried toxic chemicals were found beneath it, is in which city?
questions.explain: A chemical company had buried waste there before the land became a school and housing site; the crisis led to the 1980 Superfund law.

questions.q: A deadly 1948 air pollution disaster, in which smog from zinc and steel works was trapped by a temperature inversion, struck which Pennsylvania town?
questions.explain: About 20 people died and thousands fell ill; the event helped spur the first federal air pollution law in 1955.

questions.q: The St. Lawrence Seaway, opened in 1959 by the U.S. and Canada, allowed oceangoing ships to reach what?
questions.explain: Locks and channels let large ships sail from the Atlantic to ports such as Chicago, Detroit and Duluth.

questions.q: The Bracero Program, which brought Mexican contract workers to U.S. farms, ended in what year?
questions.explain: About 4.6 million contracts were signed from 1942 to 1964; its end helped farmworker organizing, such as the United Farm Workers.

questions.q: Operation Bootstrap, launched in the late 1940s, sought to industrialize which place, even as many of its people migrated to New York?
questions.explain: Tax breaks drew factories, but jobs could not keep up with population, and hundreds of thousands moved to the mainland.

questions.q: The Indian Relocation Act of 1956 encouraged Native Americans to do what?
options: Move from reservations to cities for jobs and training
Return to homelands in the Southeast
Enlist in the armed forces for land grants
Form tribal governments with written constitutions
questions.explain: Many relocated to Chicago, Denver, Los Angeles and other cities; programs often fell short, but urban Native communities grew.

questions.q: The Delano grape strike, begun in 1965, was started by which group of farmworkers before Cesar Chavez's union joined?
questions.explain: Larry Itliong's Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee walked out first; the groups later merged into the United Farm Workers.

questions.q: In 1956, trucking businessman Malcom McLean shipped cargo in a way that transformed world trade. What was it?
options: Refrigerated railcars that crossed by ferry
Cargo jets that carried freight overnight
Standard containers lifted from trucks onto ships
Pipelines that carried goods in slurry
questions.explain: Containerization slashed loading costs and times and later reshaped ports and global manufacturing.

questions.q: The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 gave top preference to which kind of immigrants?
options: Relatives of U.S. citizens and residents
questions.explain: Family reunification created chain migration that greatly increased immigration from Asia and Latin America.

questions.q: The Cuban Adjustment Act of 1966 allowed Cuban migrants to do what?
options: Travel freely back and forth between Cuba and the U.S.
Apply for permanent residency after a set time in the U.S.
Enter only through a Florida refugee quota
questions.explain: The waiting period, first two years and cut to one in 1976, reflected Cold War policy toward Castro's government.

questions.q: The Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act of 1971, passed partly to clear the way for an oil pipeline, gave Alaska Natives what?
options: About 44 million acres and nearly $1 billion
Seats reserved in the state legislature
A single reservation covering the interior
Full ownership of the North Slope oil fields
questions.explain: Land and money went to regional and village Native corporations, an approach unlike the reservation system.

questions.q: The Wild and Scenic Rivers Act of 1968 did what?
options: Protected chosen free-flowing rivers from dams
Gave states control of river pollution
Opened river corridors to oil drilling
Funded new dams on western rivers
questions.explain: It created a national system of protected rivers, a reaction to the era of big dam building.

questions.q: In the 1950s, conservationists including the Sierra Club blocked a proposed dam at Echo Park inside which national monument?
questions.explain: The victory boosted the modern environmental movement, though the compromise allowed Glen Canyon Dam to be built.

questions.q: The Airline Deregulation Act of 1978, signed by Jimmy Carter, did what?
options: Phased out federal control of fares and routes
questions.explain: Fares fell and air travel grew, but several major carriers failed; the Civil Aeronautics Board closed in 1985.

questions.q: Pan Am's 1958 transatlantic flights with which airliner launched the American jet age?
questions.explain: The 707 sharply cut flight times across the Atlantic; the propeller-driven DC-3 and Constellation and the later 747 jumbo jet belong to other eras.

questions.q: In 1975, the first large wave of Vietnamese refugees was processed through U.S. camps such as which California Marine base?
questions.explain: Camps at Camp Pendleton, Fort Chaffee, Eglin Air Force Base and Fort Indiantown Gap housed about 130,000 refugees.

questions.q: Which 1990 law, passed after the Exxon Valdez spill, required new oil tankers in U.S. waters to have double hulls?
questions.explain: The law also made oil companies liable for cleanup costs and authorized use of the federal Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund.

questions.q: The Sagebrush Rebellion of the late 1970s and 1980s was a movement that sought what?
options: An end to federal irrigation subsidies for farms
Transfer of federal western lands to the states
More national parks in the desert West
Higher grazing fees on public land
questions.explain: Ranchers and others resented federal land rules in states where Washington owned much of the land; Reagan declared himself a supporter.

questions.q: Interior Secretary James Watt (1981-1983) drew fierce criticism from environmentalists for what?
options: Opening public land to mining, drilling and logging
Creating dozens of new wilderness areas
Raising fees for cattle grazing on federal land
questions.explain: Watt's policies boosted membership in environmental groups; he resigned in 1983 after an offensive remark.

questions.q: The 1990 listing of the northern spotted owl as a threatened species sharply cut what in the Pacific Northwest?
questions.explain: The jobs-versus-environment fight led to the 1994 Northwest Forest Plan, which reduced federal timber harvests.

questions.q: The United States signed the 1997 Kyoto Protocol on greenhouse gases but never did what?
options: Join the United Nations climate body
questions.explain: The Clinton administration never submitted it for a vote, and George W. Bush rejected it in 2001.

questions.q: In Plyler v. Doe (1982), the Supreme Court ruled that states could not do what?
options: Require English-only classes in all public schools
Deny free public schooling to undocumented children
questions.explain: A Texas law had let districts bar such children; the Court held 5-4 that this violated equal protection.

questions.q: After the 2020 census, which state gained two House seats, the most of any state?
questions.explain: Population growth in the Sun Belt shifted seats south and west; California lost a seat for the first time.

questions.q: Hydraulic fracturing and horizontal drilling in shale helped the U.S. become the world's top producer of what by 2018?
questions.explain: The shale boom raised U.S. output past Russia and Saudi Arabia, while raising concerns about water, earthquakes and emissions.

questions.q: After Flint, Michigan, changed its water source in 2014, residents were exposed to high levels of which metal?
questions.explain: River water was not treated to prevent corrosion, so lead leached from old pipes; the crisis raised issues of race and poverty.

questions.q: In 2016, the Standing Rock Sioux led mass protests against which project, fearing it would threaten their water and sacred sites?
questions.explain: Thousands camped near the Missouri River crossing; the pipeline was completed in 2017 after court fights.

questions.q: Which pipeline, meant to carry oil from Alberta's oil sands, was rejected by Obama in 2015 and lost its permit under Biden in 2021?
questions.explain: Trump revived the project in 2017, but Biden revoked its permit on his first day, and the company ended it later in 2021.

questions.q: In 1996, Bill Clinton used the Antiquities Act to create which national monument in southern Utah?
questions.explain: The 1.7-million-acre designation angered many Utah officials; Bears Ears followed under Obama in 2016.

questions.q: Which volcano in Washington State erupted on May 18, 1980, killing 57 people?
questions.explain: The eruption blew away the mountain's north face and is the deadliest volcanic event in U.S. history.

questions.q: The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake struck the San Francisco Bay Area just before a game of which event?
questions.explain: Live broadcast from Candlestick Park carried the news; a double-deck freeway collapsed in Oakland.

questions.q: Hmong refugees, many of whom had fought for the U.S. in the secret war in Laos, resettled in large numbers in California and which state?
questions.explain: The Twin Cities area has one of the largest Hmong communities in the country, alongside California's Central Valley.

questions.q: The cluster of computer and internet companies around Santa Clara County, California, is known by what name?
questions.explain: The name comes from the silicon used in computer chips; Route 128 near Boston and North Carolina's Research Triangle are other tech hubs.

questions.q: By the 1980s, the old industrial region around the Great Lakes, which lost many factory jobs, was nicknamed what?
questions.explain: Steel and auto plants closed or moved, and population shifted toward the Sun Belt.

questions.q: After Hurricane Katrina in 2005, which city sheltered thousands of New Orleans evacuees in its Astrodome?
questions.explain: Many evacuees settled permanently in Houston and elsewhere, and New Orleans lost a large share of its population.
